assumptions: A narrow service zone produces enough independent overflow incidents to use reserved hours efficiently.
Qualified technicians will sign enforceable capacity reservations at rates compatible with installer pricing.
Installers will permit a neutral subcontractor to work without jeopardizing warranties or customer trust.
Triage and dispatch coverage can be delegated while preserving first-visit quality.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Several paid independent installer pilots with historical incident logs, reservation utilization, travel time, first-visit resolution, warranty acceptance, response-time improvement, churn, and fully loaded contribution margin.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Pre-reserving replaceable technician capacity before promising an overflow SLA is a concrete control mechanism for a lumpy service problem, not merely a lead marketplace.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Backlogs, absences, callbacks, and resolution delays are measurable installer problems, but neither incident density nor willingness to pay a fixed reservation fee has been demonstrated.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Advance reservation revenue and dispatch spread are understandable, yet utilization, travel, failed visits, correlated peaks, quality credits, and dispatcher cost can quickly erase the proposed margin.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: A large Polish installed base and a defined regional installer segment provide a plausible beachhead, although the relevant overflow incidence and serviceable radius remain unmeasured.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Local response density and neutral multi-brand service may differentiate the offer, but manufacturers, wholesalers, large installers, and informal subcontractor networks can compete or bundle coverage.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: The model can extend by postcode and from PV into batteries and heat pumps, but each expansion requires local labor, qualification, routing density, and operational supervision.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Dispatch density, failure codes, and first-visit outcomes can improve capacity placement, but technician reservations are short, nonexclusive, and replaceable.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: The founder has relevant analytical skills and a lawful discovery relationship, but no technician capacity, external installer contracts, or demonstrated field-service operating advantage exists yet.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Poland's very large, aging prosumer installation base should increase aftercare surface area, even though the packet does not establish current overflow growth or fault frequency.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Public installer registers, wholesalers, technician referrals, and a separately contracted discovery pilot offer concrete low-cost routes, though none has yet produced paid independent demand.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: Safety, warranty authorization, travel, quality control, peak correlation, phone coverage, and dependence on a paid dispatcher create substantial operational risk for a part-time founder.

highest_value_structural_change: Constrain the launch to one equipment category and compact postcode cluster, reserve only OEM-authorized technician blocks, and sell a prepaid pilot SLA with delegated dispatch and explicit first-visit-quality guarantees.
main_structural_strength: The venture can obtain bounded control of supply through explicit capacity reservations and sell a measurable response commitment to installers while leaving end-customer ownership intact.
primary_score_limiter: The economics depend on unmeasured local incident density and utilization, while reliable execution may demand an always-on field operation inconsistent with the founder's available time.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Installers may reject third-party repair as a quality, warranty, and customer-relationship risk, and public certification alone does not establish technician competence or availability.
